svg.title: Ray time on the head and worker pods
svg.text: Ray on the head and workers: workflow, functions, line numbers and measured times
Code: ej-prj-i4-1 925abd467, Ray 2.56.1. One sky launch (run 5 of 6) on 6 pods on k8s/kind-skypilot, one echo. Clock times are seconds from the start of sky launch.
The letter beside a time says where it comes from. Time ranges cover the 5 worker pods. The timeline is at the bottom.

ray start, raylet, per-job Ray workers
Almost all Python start and imports for the ray CLI. GCS itself takes
tens of ms. Workers wait for this port.
Wait for the dashboard, then raylet
ray start polls every 0.1 s until the dashboard publishes its address.
This delays the workers too, through the head's node record.
The raylet blocks until the dashboard agent writes its ports.
Sets when the Ray wait begins. Runtime setup was 1.6–24.1 s across 6
launches, likely from the uv dry-run stalls found earlier; not checked
Set by the head's imports. ray start begins within 0.08 s of GCS
Poll for the head's node record
With the 0.2 s poll patch, this is now a real wait for the head to
register, not wasted sleep: workers notice it 0.15 s later.
Raylet waits for the dashboard agent
No sleep to shorten: 0 sleeps before the port was written, in 6
launches. The raylet polls the port file every 50 ms in C++. The time is
Skylet start, and wait for all 6 nodes
These run together, and the launch waits for both.
Setup between Ray and the job
SkyPilot, not Ray: two Python commands on the head, mostly imports. This
launch sets no autostop; a managed job also runs set_autostop here.
home directory echo, rsync job script
Largest fixed cost in the job: import sky loads the whole backend,
though the driver uses five modules.

Head ray start → last worker registered

Six sky launch runs on 6 pods, code ej-prj-i4-1 925abd467 (0.2 s head-node poll), Ray 2.56.1, kind on one machine, so all pods share a clock. The timeline is one real launch; the table shows how much each stage

varies. Runtime setup was 2.64, 3.31 and 1.62 s in three launches, and 6.73, 11.51 and 24.1 s in the others, likely uv dry-run stalls, which these runs did not check. There is no comparison or significance test
No sleep to shorten in the raylet's wait for the dashboard agent: no agent recorded a sleep before writing its port, in any launch, and the raylet polls the port file every 50 ms in C++
(src/ray/util/port_persistence.h). The time is the agent's Python start and imports, plus get_all_modules importing every module under ray.dashboard.modules.

The trace image adds timers to every Python process. Never benchmark latency with it. Who called whom in S rows is inferred from sent and received counts in an earlier trace. Not shown: tasks with setup,
